rv.q: Sean Hayes delivers a tour-de-force performance as Oscar Levant in this biographical play that captures both the wit and tragedy of the pianist-comedian's life.
For anyone who cherishes personal freedom or Hayes himself, it's not to be missed.
Such is the magic of 'Good Night, Oscar' and, specifically, actor Sean Hayes' virtuosic turn as the accomplished Jewish pianist and talk show personality riddled with various mental illnesses.
“Good Night, Oscar” provides a vehicle for Hayes to be snappy and tragic.
Though the play itself may not be memorable, Hayes’ acting feat undoubtedly is.
Instead, it offers a spray of Levant’s most famous quips, like the one about Elizabeth Taylor: “Always a bride, never a bridesmaid.”
That thrilling moment — without mannerisms, words, other characters or exposition — is the only time Levant and “Good Night, Oscar” come to life.
I would not recommend showing up an hour and twenty minutes into a Broadway show, but it sure would be nice if you could do that at Good Night, Oscar.
There is a perhaps overused but most apt phrase to describe what is happening on stage at the Belasco, and that is "tour de force."
Sean Hayes is just too easy to love.
In Good Night, Oscar, Levant is a harbinger of pop-culture, for good and ill, to come—and the demons of all kinds that have shaped it.
Like this production, it proves that a gifted performer can lift the spirit against all odds.
It’s a stunning interpretation.
Good Night, Oscar is less than convincing.
Unfortunately, there were few other highlights for me in this workmanlike production
To call Hayes’ work here “a tour-de-force” performance is accurate, while not really doing it justice.
It's a satisfying evening all around.

Though Doug Wright’s Good Night, Oscar may not tell you all you want to know about its characters, it gives Sean Hayes a tour de force in the role of wit and hypochondriac Oscar Levant and he lives up to its potential, giving what may be the best performance on Broadway at this moment.
He is incomparable, acicular as barbed wire in his humor and flooring when he shows his bravery, which is to say the wounded soul beneath the proud man.
Hayes was a revelation, both in his performance and his playing.

Too much of ’Good Night, Oscar’ is devoted to Levant and Paar’s famous one-liners...Certainly the audience laughs throughout. But they don’t do much for the play dramatically. We wish we knew more about Oscar Levant before saying goodnight.
Other than that it is a hodge-podge of disappointing writing and direction.
As presented here, though, neither the man, nor his problems, provide a prescription for theatrical wellness.
